item.title: CoMLRL Quick Start
item.description:
This tutorial demonstrates a simple two-agent training task with a length-ratio reward. Both agents receive the same prompt and generate independently; the second agent does not see the first agent’s response. The reward encourages the second output to contain 2–3× as many characters as the first. It does not evaluate story quality or semantic collaboration.

Run the example directly from an installed source checkout:

python examples/story-len-ratio.py

Memory requirements depend on the model, number of agents, batch size, and response length. W&B logging is disabled by default. To enable it, add --wandb (and optionally --wandb-project or --wandb-entity) to the command above.

item.title: Installation
item.description:
CoMLRL provides several different ways for installation. Python 3.10 or later is required. Install a PyTorch build compatible with your machine separately; it is intentionally excluded from the package’s core dependencies.

These docs describe the current source checkout. Published PyPI and conda-forge packages can lag behind it, so use the source installation for features added on the clean-up branch.

Install from PyPI#

pip install comlrl
# install PyTorch compatible with your device

Install from conda-forge#

conda install -c conda-forge comlrl
# install PyTorch compatible with your device

item.title: Multi-Agent REINFORCE
item.description:
REINFORCE is a class of policy gradient methods that optimize the policy directly using sampled returns. It has been widely used to fine-tune LLMs because of its simplicity and efficiency, e.g., GRPO, Dr. GRPO, RLOO, ReMax, TreeRPO, and REINFORCE++. REINFORCE can be extended to multi-agent settings, where multiple LLM agents respond at each turn and their joint responses receive a shared reward.

item.title: Training Paradigms
item.description:
An actor generates the responses being learned; an iterative comparator supplies alternative responses to the same task. Choose their generation layouts separately from the comparator’s policy source. Both layouts can be used with the MADPO and MARLHF objectives.

Collaboration Modes#

collaboration_mode determines the trainable actor layout. comparator_generation_mode determines the comparator layout in iterative training.

Actor layout Comparator layout Joint responses
Decentralized Decentralized Each role generates its own response on both sides of the comparison.
Decentralized Centralized Separate actors are compared with one comparator that writes all roles’ responses.
Centralized Centralized One actor and one comparator each write a complete joint response.

In decentralized mode, each agent has its own policy and generates its own response. MADPO combines their preference margins, while MARLHF learns one reward from the joint responses.

item.title: Comparator
item.description:
A comparator supplies candidate responses for MADPOIterTrainer and MARLHFIterTrainer. The trainer compares current-policy and comparator responses at the same candidate index. Either side can win; tied rewards do not form a preference pair.

Choose the source with comparator_policy. Choose whether it generates separate role responses or one joint response in Training Paradigms.

Policy Sources#

Policy Response source
current Active actor weights, sampled with a separate comparator random-number stream.
current_copy Current actor weights, with optional placement on separate comparator devices.
model Explicit model identifiers or model sources supplied for the comparator.
history A saved earlier actor checkpoint.
api A remote model endpoint.

current is the default. current_copy uses the same policy weights; when comparator and actor devices match, it reuses the actor models. With separate devices, the comparator copies are prepared for that iteration’s collection phase and released afterward.

item.title: Model Loading & Saving
item.description:
CoMLRL supports both homogeneous and heterogeneous models. Users can assign agent_model/critic_model with HuggingFace model identifiers for homogeneous setups, or provide agents/critics lists for heterogeneous setups.

Local model directories are also supported. You can save trained actors, load their weights into a new trainer, and train them further. The sections below cover model loading, the saved directory layout, and which training state must be initialized again.

The examples below assume you have defined a task-specific reward_func and train_dataset, as shown in the quick start. They use num_turns=1; multi-turn training additionally requires an external_transition.

item.title: Multi-Agent Actor-Critic
item.description:
Actor-Critic (AC) methods are widely-used policy gradient methods that employ critics to facilitate training. AC methods can achieve lower variance and better sample efficiency than REINFORCE, but this requires careful design and tuning of the critic to ensure stable training. In Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), Actor-Critic methods can be instantiated as Multi-Agent Actor-Critic (MAAC) and Independent Actor-Critic (IAC).

MAAC#

Multi-Agent Actor-Critic (MAAC) uses one Centralized Critic (CC) across agents to evaluate joint histories with critic_type="v", or joint history-action pairs with critic_type="q". The critic receives the agents’ prompts joined into one text; Q mode also includes their generated completions.

item.title: Dataset Loading
item.description:
Keep task inputs and metadata together in a dataset and reserve a separate evaluation split. This guide uses the length-ratio task from the quick start to prepare data for training and evaluation.

Dataset Splits#

Each dataset row is a dictionary. The default formatter reads its prompt field; additional fields can hold targets, labels, test cases, or other information needed by your reward function. Trainers pass the original row to the reward function through batch_items.

item.title: Replay Buffer
item.description:
Iterative preference training collects a new set of comparison pairs each round. The replay buffer decides which collected pairs are used for that round’s updates. It is shared by MADPOIterTrainer and MARLHFIterTrainer.

The current round is written before replay selection, so it is eligible alongside earlier rounds. Replay controls the training data; the comparator policy controls how new candidate responses are generated.

Replay Modes#

Mode Eligible preference data
current All pairs from the current round, without historical sampling.
nearest_k The latest preference_replay_k non-empty iteration datasets, including the current one when non-empty.
all_history Every recorded non-empty iteration dataset in the current trainer run.
lambda_decay The same history, with greater sampling weight on more recent datasets when λ is below 1.

nearest_k means recent iterations in time. It does not perform nearest-neighbor retrieval by embedding or similarity.

item.title: Logging Metric
item.description:
Save evaluation results locally, record training curves in Weights & Biases, and add task-specific metrics. The examples below build on the trainer and held-out split in Dataset Loading.

Local Metrics#

Evaluation returns a metrics dictionary even when W&B is disabled. Save it locally if you only need a record of a completed evaluation:

import json
from pathlib import Path

# Use the MAGRPO trainer and eval_dataset from the Dataset Loading guide.
metrics = trainer.evaluate(num_eval_samples=len(eval_dataset))
Path("eval-metrics.json").write_text(json.dumps(metrics, indent=2) + "\n")

item.title: Multi-Turn Interaction
item.description:
Many complex problems cannot be solved in a single turn. LLM agents need to interact with the environment to obtain useful feedback from other models or tools involved in the system.

Multi-Turn MAGRPO#

MAGRPO in the multi-turn setting forms a tree-structured rollout expansion where branches represent different joint responses (TreeRPO).

In each episode, a task is sampled from the dataset to construct initial observations \( \mathbf{o}_0=\{o_{1, 0}, \cdots, o_{n, 0}\} \) and histories \( \mathbf{h}_0=\{h_{1, 0}, \cdots, h_{n, 0}\} \) for all agents. At each turn, agents generate a group of joint responses \( \mathbf{a}^{\mathcal{G}}_t\gets\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\mathcal{G}}(\cdot|\mathbf{h}_t) \) from their current observation-action history \( \mathbf{h}_t \), with each response initiating a distinct rollout. Agents receive joint rewards \( r^{(g)}_{t} \) for each response based on the accumulated history \( \mathbf{a}^{(g)}_{t} \in \mathbf{a}^{\mathcal{G}}_{t} \) and current action. Each rollout then evolves independently, producing new joint observations \( \mathbf{o}^{\mathcal{G}}_{t+1} \) as the environment dynamics unfold and spawning more rollouts at the next turn \( t+1 \). This process continues until the terminal turn is reached \( H \).

item.title: Training Parallelization
item.description:
CoMLRL trainers run in a Python process. For IAC, parallel_training="none" is the default; "mp" enables scheduling agents and critics on explicitly assigned devices. Neither mode requires a job scheduler.

Model Parallelization#

Pass an IACConfig to your IACTrainer through its args parameter. For example, with four visible CUDA devices and two agents:

from comlrl.trainers.actor_critic import IACConfig

config = IACConfig(
 num_agents=2,
 num_turns=1,
 use_separate_critic=True,
 parallel_training="mp",
 agent_devices=["cuda:0", "cuda:1"],
 critic_devices=["cuda:2", "cuda:3"],
)

agent_devices is required in "mp" mode. critic_devices is also required when use_separate_critic=True. Each model stays on its assigned device; this does not split an individual model across GPUs. Responses are passed to the reward function and rewards are used for each agent’s update.

item.title: Developer
item.description:
Support#

We are willing to help you with any issues you encounter while using CoMLRL.

Report Issues#

If you are stuck with a problem using CoMLRL, please follow this procedure:

  1. Read the documentation first, including using the search feature (Ctrl + K).

  2. Search the GitHub Issues archives to see if someone else already had the same problem.

  3. Before writing, try to create a minimal example that reproduces the problem. You’ll get the fastest response if you can send just a handful of lines of code that show what isn’t working.
